title: The hands-on slot
objective: See where a browser lab sits in a lesson, and how it takes over the screen when you actually start working in it.

blocks.text: A lab is the one thing that genuinely belongs embedded. It is not something to read — it is somewhere to work, and it has to be inside the lesson so that finishing it can count towards your progress.

In the flow of the lesson it sits at a comfortable size, so you can see it alongside the instructions. The moment you start typing in it, that size stops being enough — which is what the expand control is for.

Not every hands-on moment deserves a full workspace. A two-minute check belongs right here in the reading, because making someone open a separate environment for it is the reason they skip it. It still expands if you want more room — the size is a starting posture, not a restriction.

blocks.title: Check who owns this file
blocks.description: One command, one answer. Small enough to do without leaving the sentence you were reading — and it opens bigger if you would rather work that way.

blocks.title: Read and fix a permission problem
blocks.description: A throwaway machine with a file the wrong people can write to. Find it and fix it. This one needs room to work, so it can fill the screen.

blocks.title: Why this is the trust mechanism
blocks.text: A quiz shows you can recognise the right answer. A lab shows you can produce it. That is what makes a required checkpoint worth requiring, and what lets someone skip other lessons with confidence.

blocks.title: What to check in this demo
steps: Press Bigger on the short exercise — it opens over the lesson, which stays visible behind it
Press Expand to full screen on the longer lab — that one takes the whole window
Press Escape from either and confirm you land back at the same place
Resize the browser narrow and check both still behave
blocks.expected: Both panels grow when you ask them to, in proportion to the work they hold, and Escape always returns you to your place in the lesson.

cheatsheet: A lab is embedded because it is somewhere to work, not something to read
Size is a starting posture, not a limit: short exercises start inline, real scenarios start large, and both expand
A short exercise opens into a dialog over the lesson; a full scenario takes the whole screen
Escape always returns you to the lesson at the same place
Doing beats recognising — the lab is what makes a required checkpoint meaningful

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a lab embedded when an article is not?

choices.B: A lab is somewhere the learner works, and completing it has to count towards progress — an article is something they read, which is better as native page content
choices.D: Articles are not part of courses

checkpoint.explanation: The split is doing versus reading. Anything interactive that feeds progress stays inside; anything to read becomes part of the page itself.

checkpoint.prompt: What should happen when the learner leaves full screen?

choices.A: They return to the course map
choices.C: They land back in the lesson at the same place

checkpoint.explanation: Losing your place is the thing that actually breaks flow. Expanding and collapsing must never cost the learner their position.

checkpoint.prompt: A lab takes two minutes. Which starting size is right?

choices.A: Full screen, so it is consistent with every other lab
choices.B: Inline in the reading, with the option to open it bigger if the learner wants
choices.C: Inline only, with no way to make it bigger
choices.D: It should not be a lab at all

checkpoint.explanation: Making someone enter a separate environment for two minutes of work is why short exercises get skipped. Starting inline removes that cost; keeping the expand control means a small screen or an awkward task is never a dead end.

challenge.title: Give the print server a fixed address
challenge.brief: The print server has to answer at {{targetIp}} every time it boots, on the 192.168.10.0/24 network with the router at 192.168.10.1. Set the interface up so that stays true, then apply it.

requirements.label: The address does not change between boots
It answers at {{targetIp}}, the address the brief asks for
The subnet matches the network it sits on
It can reach the rest of the network
The settings are applied, not just typed in

challenge.debrief: A fixed address is what makes a print queue findable. With DHCP the lease can change and every workstation pointing at the old address quietly stops printing.
